text: The samples were collected in March.
Two hundred seedlings were assessed at baseline.
Contamination was ruled out in the second trial.
The effect has been observed in three independent trials.
Growth was assessed every seven days.
The plants were not watered for six days.
The authors conclude that the evidence suggests a seasonal effect.

The mistake I made in my first year, and I watch new students make it every single semester, was reading a paper the way I read a chapter of a book. Word one to word ten thousand, in order, with a dictionary open. It took me an entire afternoon to get through one paper and by the end I could not have told you what the study actually found. So somebody in my lab sat me down and gave me an order that sounded almost rude. Read the last sentence of the background, then read the results, then stop. If those two do not interest you, close the tab. You have lost ninety seconds instead of four hours. And if they do interest you, then go back and read the method properly, because that is where you find out whether you believe the results at all. It felt wrong for about two weeks and then it felt obvious. Now I probably open thirty abstracts a week and I read maybe two papers properly, and that ratio is not laziness. That is the job.

Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the journal club. Before we start, three quick things about how this session runs, because we have several new people today. First, the paper was circulated on Monday and it is assumed that everybody has read at least the abstract and the figures. You are not expected to have read the entire discussion. Second, we go section by section, and the rule is that we talk about the method before we talk about the results. Every year somebody wants to argue about the conclusions in the first five minutes, and every year that conversation goes nowhere, because you cannot judge a finding until you know how it was measured. Third, and this is the one people find uncomfortable at first: anybody may say that they did not understand a section. Nobody here has read everything, and the person who admits that the baseline was not clear to them is usually the person who has spotted a real problem with the paper. We finish at half past four.
